summary: The note follows Emily Torres, a third-grade teacher with asthma, to illustrate how urban air pollution harms public health in her city. It cites a UPHI study showing particulates 40% above WHO safe levels, and explains that industry, traffic and many minor sources all contribute. It covers the personal and economic costs and ends with community action and city policy efforts toward cleaner air.
one_line: A teacher's asthma struggles illustrate how urban air pollution harms health and costs families, and how community and policy action are responding.
key_facts: Emily Torres, a third-grade teacher on the metropolitan east side, had an asthma attack on Monday, October 17, 2023, as she turned onto Maple Street.
A September 5, 2023 study by the Urban Public Health Institute (UPHI) found airborne particulates 40% above what the World Health Organization deems safe.
Hospital admissions for asthma and COPD have trended upward in recent years.
Dr. Karen Liu, who leads the pulmonology department at Greenfield Hospital, said "this city's air is concocting a breathing crisis."
PM2.5 is particulate matter under 2.5 micrometers in diameter and can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.
Industrial activity and vehicular traffic are the prime culprits of poor air quality, but construction sites and waste burning also contribute.

On November 12, 2023, environmental watchdog EarthGuard, led by activist Michael Chen, reported that minor emission sources such as garden bonfires, diesel generators and bakery ovens collectively worsen pollution.
Emily Torres plans her day around pollution forecasts, avoiding jogging and open-air cafes on bad days.
Health economist Frank Robinson estimates the healthcare burden of pollution-related diseases at billions annually, with families bearing part through medical expenses and lost income.
Even with health insurance, Emily Torres's co-pays for asthma medication and doctor visits strain her resources.
The ClearAir Initiative, started by citizens such as Sandra Gibson, plants trees, organizes car-free days and educates about domestic practices affecting air quality.
The city's Urban Development Authority (UDA) is pursuing green corridors and stricter vehicular emissions testing, alongside electric buses and biking lanes.
The city council's emission regulations are slow and entangled in legal and political disputes.
